u1-emuA:
(When someone proposes an experiment in trying something different, it doesn't have to be that everybody who wants to try that new thing has to buy new land right away. First they can try it within the parent group, then in a semi-autonomous way, and then on nearby land as a seed group that shares some resources (tool library, child care, business skills, friendships, etc.). Full fission is only one point on a gradient of options.)

Some experiments aren't viable unless they can have enough land, etc. from the start. Sometimes an experiment in a new rule set won't look good if it doesn't have the right infrastructure to support it.
u1-emuB:
In many cases, it might be better to try out the different rule, first within the parent group, or semi-autonomously close to the parent group, or as a nearby seed with some tools and/or child care and/or business or friendship connections, etc. Fission should be seen as one point along a gradient of closeness, not as a prerequisite for experimentation.

Sometimes, experiments aren’t viable unless they are “nourished” with a certain amount of land, or a certain number of people, or certain other rules that help it to function. It might not be possible to “prove” that a new idea is better in a small, inexpensive, low-risk experiment.

u3-emuA: (Just for the record, the Federation of Egalitarian Communities is rebuilding right now.) Some notes on the somewhat dry topic of building federations: A federation, like any institution, takes work. Federation-level delegates, records, compliance, resource coordination, meetings, succession, and whatever functions the federation is asked to handle will soak up some of the labor and material resources of the communities, before local crises have had a chance to. If the larger legal or economic system demands it, the federation will need a budget of external money. It may be that not all of this work should be done under one institutional roof: bilateral friendships, local clusters, and/or institutions that handle specific functions can coexist with a general federation. For instance, the Federation of Egalitarian Communities' current health pool, PEACH, is governed separately from the FEC delegates.
u3-emuB: (This is the Federation of Egalitarian Communities, currently in the process of rebuilding.) Federations take work. If the federation is doing anything, it’s going to take up labor and material resources in the communities involved, even before any crisis arises. There will be delegates, records to keep, compliance issues, resource coordination, meetings, succession issues, and whatever other work needs to be done for the functions the federation accepts responsibility for. If the external system requires it, they’ll probably need to budget for external cash sources to pay for what they do. That said, different functions might be handled by different institutions. Bilateral friendship relations, local area clusters, and function-specific institutions can all co-exist with a general-purpose federation. For instance, the FEC’s current health insurance pooling arrangement (PEACH) has a separate governance from the FEC delegates.
u4-emuA: Related to the point about not requiring cooperation to become assimilation, one thing the FEC does that might be a good model is to have not just members, but also communities that are on a path towards becoming members, and also Friends of the FEC that can remain just that indefinitely. The idea is to make it as easy as possible for people to move between communities, but if every community had identical procedures for membership and housing assignments and health care and recordkeeping and labor accounting and travel cost sharing and taxes and transition conflict resolution... well, instead of trying to harmonize all those internal procedures, it's probably better just to have a thin interface between communities that defines who is responsible for what.
u4-emuB: To add to this, it might also be wise to be careful that, in working together, different communities don't end up being forced to become more the same. Right now, the FEC allows for different kinds of relationship: full membership, working towards full membership, or being a Friend of the FEC. Between communities, people should be able to move relatively easily if they want to. But often, the administrative systems that different communities have internally don't need to be made the same, just to have someone take responsibility for dealing with the interface: where will the person live when s/he first gets to the new community; what is their initial status, how will health care and other records be handled, will any labor be counted, who will pay for travel expenses, taxes, etc. It doesn't need to be hard, but someone has to be responsible for thinking about it and dealing with it when transitions happen.
u5-emuA: Would there be a need for money between them? When somebody exchanges something with somebody else, or takes on an obligation to somebody else, it needs to be clear whether that is done as a gift, as part of a pooling of resources such as food or medicine, as a loan of something like a vehicle or tool, as reciprocal labor, as an emergency housing arrangement, as part of a shared building project, as a visit primarily for training and/or relationship building, or whatever. Even if the interface to the outside is in cash, and even if cash is used to acquire goods and services from the outside, it would still be necessary to keep separate account of the money going out to or on behalf of another community as a grant, as a loan, as a guarantee, as a shared enterprise commitment, or whatever. Just as solidarity does not mean unlimited joint liability for obligations to the outside, it does not mean unlimited claim on labor, stores, land, tools, or whatever. Even within a federation, there would need to be purpose-specific accounting, even if not in terms of prices or parity.
u5-emuB: What do accounting professionals think about this? There is no reason for an internal monetary system, however it is vital to be able to distinguish between mutually beneficial exchanges and non-binding and binding obligations that may arise in the course of everyday life (distinguishing a gift, contribution to a common pool, loan, trade, barter, joint construction project, visit for training/relationship purposes, etc). This is entirely possible without a monetary system or parity, just purpose specific accounting. If cash is being used at the interface, then there is no reason why one could not have grants, loans, guarantees, and shared enterprise commitments. This is not unlimited mutual liability or claim on each others labor, stores, real estate, tools, etc.
u6-emuA: If two principles contradict, keep the hard case, with all information about what happened, what principles were involved, what the first judgments were, what the final judgment reasoning was, any dissent, what the consequences were, and what version of the rule this is. If the rule changes, re-run the hard case.
u6-emuB: To prevent the law from gradually sliding into a bland “average” of the principles it represents, at least a few hard cases should be recorded, in which the principles collide. For each such case, the facts, the colliding principles, the first instance decision, the final decision with its motivation, possible dissent, consequences of the case, and the version of the rule that this case defines, should be recorded. Whenever a new version of a rule is made, the hard cases should be run again.
